content: The references provided are a comprehensive list of studies, trials, and guidelines related to pediatric emergency care, particularly focusing on the management of seizures, febrile convulsions, and respiratory conditions in children. 1. Adhikari et al. (2013) analyzed the clinical profiles of children admitted with seizures in a tertiary care hospital in Western Nepal, providing insights into the epidemiology and management of pediatric seizures in that region. 2. The Advanced Paediatric Life Support (Australia, 2012) manual outlines practical approaches to pediatric life support, emphasizing evidence-based techniques for managing critically ill children. 3. Agarwal et al. (2007) conducted a randomized study comparing intravenous valproate and phenytoin in the treatment of status epilepticus, highlighting the efficacy and safety profiles of these medications. 4. Ahmad et al. (2006) compared intranasal lorazepam and intramuscular paraldehyde for prolonged convulsions in children, demonstrating the effectiveness and safety of intranasal lorazepam in an open randomized trial. 5. Akpede and Sykes (1993) investigated febrile seizures of acute onset in school-aged children in Benin City, Nigeria, providing valuable data on the clinical presentation and outcomes. 6. Akpede et al. (1992) evaluated the indications for lumbar puncture in children presenting with convulsions and fever in a Nigerian emergency room, offering guidance on diagnostic decision-making. 7. Akpede et al. (1993a) studied the patterns of infections in children under six years old presenting with febrile seizures in Benin City, Nigeria, identifying common infectious triggers. 8. Akpede et al. (1993b) explored the relationship between febrile seizures and malaria, questioning whether these seizures indicate cerebral involvement or are simply febrile in nature. 9. Alario et al. (1995) examined the relationship between oxygen saturation and clinical assessment in acutely wheezing infants and children, emphasizing the importance of objective measures in respiratory distress. 10. Alvarez et al. (2011) compared second-line treatments for status epilepticus, including phenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam, providing evidence for their relative efficacy and safety. 11. Alvarez et al. (2012) investigated the role of comorbidities in predicting outcomes after status epilepticus, highlighting the impact of underlying conditions on prognosis. 12. The American Academy of Pediatrics (2008) published clinical practice guidelines for the long-term management of children with simple febrile seizures, offering evidence-based recommendations. 13. The American Academy of Pediatrics (1996) provided guidelines for the neurodiagnostic evaluation of children with a first simple febrile seizure, emphasizing appropriate use of diagnostic tools. 14. Aneja (2012) reviewed the use of benzodiazepines for acute seizure management, discussing their efficacy and safety in pediatric populations. 15. Annegers et al. (1987) identified prognostic factors for unprovoked seizures following febrile convulsions, contributing to risk stratification in affected children. 16. Anon. (1980) summarized an NIH consensus statement on the long-term management of children with febrile seizures, providing a foundational reference for clinical practice. 17. Appleton et al. (1995) compared lorazepam and diazepam for the acute treatment of epileptic seizures and status epilepticus, demonstrating the advantages of lorazepam in certain scenarios. 18. Appleton et al. (2008) reviewed drug management strategies for acute tonic-clonic convulsions and convulsive status epilepticus in children, synthesizing evidence from multiple studies. 19. Armon et al. (2003) developed evidenceand consensus-based guidelines for managing children after a seizure, providing a structured approach to postictal care. 20. The Australian and New Zealand Resuscitation Councils (2011) outlined techniques in pediatric advanced life support, emphasizing updated resuscitation guidelines. 21. Autret et al. (1990) conducted a double-blind, randomized trial comparing diazepam and placebo for preventing recurrent febrile seizures, demonstrating the efficacy of diazepam. 22. Bacon et al. (1981a) studied the behavioral effects of phenobarbital and phenytoin in young children, highlighting potential cognitive and behavioral side effects. 23. Bacon et al. (1981b) conducted a placebo-controlled study on the prophylactic use of phenobarbital and phenytoin for febrile convulsions, providing evidence for their effectiveness. 24. Bajaj et al. (2005) reported on the use of intermittent clobazam for febrile seizures in an Indian cohort, demonstrating its utility in seizure prevention. 25. Binger (1928) investigated the role of oxygen inhalation in relieving anoxemia in pneumonia, laying the groundwork for modern respiratory support strategies. 26. Blume (2003) reviewed the diagnosis and management of epilepsy, providing a comprehensive overview of current practices. 27. Bressan et al. (2013) evaluated high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy for bronchiolitis in a pediatric ward, demonstrating its feasibility and effectiveness. 28. Brevoord et al. (2005) analyzed a treatment protocol for status epilepticus based on midazolam and phenytoin, providing clinical insights into protocol-based management. 29. Camfield et al. (1979) examined the side effects of phenobarbital in toddlers, focusing on behavioral and cognitive aspects. 30. Camfield et al. (1980) studied the prevention of recurrent febrile seizures using antipyretic instructions combined with phenobarbital or placebo, offering evidence for preventive strategies. 31. Canagarayar and Soysa (1987) discussed the management of febrile seizures in a developing country, highlighting resource-limited approaches. 32. Chamberlain and Gorman (1988) investigated occult bacteremia in children with simple febrile seizures, emphasizing the importance of identifying underlying infections. 33. Chamberlain et al. (2014) compared lorazepam and diazepam for pediatric status epilepticus in a randomized clinical trial, providing evidence for their relative efficacy. 34. Chang et al. (2010) studied intravenous valproate for seizures in Taiwanese children, comparing outcomes in valproate-naïve and non-naïve patients. 35. Chen et al. (2009) evaluated intravenous sodium valproate for diazepam-refractory convulsive status epilepticus in mainland China, demonstrating its effectiveness. 36. Chisti et al. (2012) identified clinical predictors and outcomes of hypoxemia in children with diarrhea and/or pneumonia in an urban hospital in Bangladesh. 37. Crawley et al. (1996) examined seizures and status epilepticus in childhood cerebral malaria, providing insights into their clinical presentation and management. 38. Crawley et al. (2000) studied the effects of phenobarbital on seizure frequency and mortality in childhood cerebral malaria, highlighting its potential risks and benefits. 39. Daugbjerg et al. (1990) compared intermittent prophylaxis with diazepam and valproic acid for febrile convulsions, providing evidence for their use. 40. De Bruin et al. (1992) analyzed acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in infants and children, describing clinical and pathological characteristics. 41. Duke et al. (2002) investigated hypoxemia in acute respiratory and non-respiratory illnesses in neonates and children in a developing country, emphasizing the need for oxygen therapy. 42. Duke et al. (2008) evaluated improved oxygen systems for childhood pneumonia in Papua New Guinea, demonstrating their effectiveness in reducing mortality. 43. The European Resuscitation Council (2005) published guidelines for resuscitation, providing a comprehensive framework for emergency care. 44. Farwell et al. (1990) studied the effects of phenobarbital on intelligence and seizure recurrence in children with febrile seizures, raising concerns about its cognitive impact. 45. Fisher et al. (2005) proposed definitions for epileptic seizures and epilepsy, standardizing terminology for clinical and research purposes. 46. Fuchs et al. (2007) published the 5th edition of the Advanced Pediatric Life Support manual, serving as a key resource for pediatric emergency medicine. 47. Garvey et al. (1998) identified children most likely to benefit from emergency brain CT scans after seizures, guiding imaging decisions. 48. Gathwala et al. (2012) compared intravenous diazepam, midazolam, and lorazepam for acute seizure control, providing evidence for their relative efficacy. 49. Gerber and Berliner (1981) discussed appropriate diagnostic evaluation for children with simple febrile seizures, emphasizing evidence-based approaches. 50. Gottwald et al. (1999) studied the prehospital stability of diazepam and lorazepam, providing insights into their use in emergency settings. 51. Gwer et al. (2012) investigated continuous EEG monitoring in Kenyan children with non-traumatic coma, highlighting its diagnostic and prognostic value. 52. Heckmatt et al. (1976) reported on the failure of phenobarbital to prevent febrile convulsions, questioning its routine use. 53. Hesdorffer et al. (2008) examined the association between MRI-detected brain abnormalities and febrile seizure type, providing insights into their pathophysiology. 54. Hough et al. (2014) studied the physiological effects of high-flow nasal cannula therapy in infants with bronchiolitis, demonstrating its benefits. 55. Idro et al. (2008) analyzed the incidence, etiology, and outcomes of acute seizures in children admitted to a rural Kenyan hospital, providing valuable epidemiological data. 56. The International League Against Epilepsy (1993) published guidelines for epidemiologic studies on epilepsy, standardizing research methodologies. 57. Kariuki et al. (2011) studied acute seizures attributable to falciparum malaria in an endemic area on the Kenyan coast, highlighting the burden of malaria-related seizures. 58. Kariuki et al. (2013) investigated the genetic risk of acute seizures in African children with falciparum malaria, identifying potential genetic markers. 59. Khosroshahi et al. (2011) compared diazepam and clobazam for intermittent prophylaxis of febrile seizures, providing evidence for their use. 60. Kleinman et al. (2010) published the 2010 American Heart Association guidelines for pediatric advanced life support, emphasizing updated resuscitation techniques. 61. Knudsen (1985a) demonstrated the effectiveness of short-term diazepam prophylaxis in febrile convulsions, providing evidence for its use. 62. Knudsen (1985b) analyzed recurrence risk after a first febrile seizure and the effect of short-term diazepam prophylaxis, guiding preventive strategies. 63. Kokwaro et al. (2003) studied the pharmacokinetics and clinical effects of phenobarbital in children with severe falciparum malaria and convulsions, providing dosing recommendations. 64. Kuile et al. (1992) investigated the absorption of intramuscular phenobarbital in children with severe falciparum malaria, highlighting its pharmacokinetic properties. 65. Kuturec et al. (1997) evaluated the utility of EEG as a predictor of febrile seizure recurrence, providing evidence for its diagnostic value. 66. Lahat et al. (2000) compared intranasal midazolam with intravenous diazepam for treating febrile seizures in children, demonstrating the effectiveness of intranasal administration. 67. Laman et al. (2005) assessed the ability of clinical signs to predict hypoxemia in children with pneumonia in Papua New Guinea, emphasizing the importance of clinical assessment. 68. Lodha et al. (2004) evaluated the accuracy of clinical symptoms and signs in predicting hypoxemia in children with acute lower respiratory tract infections, guiding diagnostic approaches. 69. Lowenstein et al. (1999) called for a revision of the definition of status epilepticus, reflecting advances in understanding and management. 70. Mackintosh (1970) studied the feasibility of prophylactic treatment for febrile convulsions, exploring the use of drugs at the first sign of fever or infection. 71. Mackway-Jones et al. (2005) published the 4th edition of the Advanced Pediatric Life Support manual, providing practical guidance for pediatric emergency care. 72. Mahyar et al. (2010) investigated the correlation between serum selenium levels and febrile seizures, identifying a potential biomarker. 73. Maitland et al. (2011) analyzed mortality after fluid bolus therapy in African children with severe infection, raising concerns about its safety. 74. Malamiri et al. (2012) compared the efficacy and safety of intravenous sodium valproate and phenobarbital in controlling convulsive status epilepticus in children, providing evidence for their use. 75. Mallewa and Birbeck (2013) reviewed the EEG findings in tropical encephalopathies, providing insights into their diagnostic utility. 76. Mamelle et al. (1984) conducted a randomized trial comparing sodium valproate, phenobarbital, and placebo for preventing recurrent febrile convulsions, demonstrating their relative efficacy. 77. Mayfield et al. (2013) reported on the use of high-flow nasal cannula therapy in pediatric respiratory support, highlighting its benefits in a case series. 78. Mayfield et al. (2014) reviewed high-flow nasal cannula therapy for respiratory support in children, synthesizing evidence from multiple studies. 79. Maytal et al. (2000) evaluated the value of early postictal EEG in children with complex febrile seizures, providing evidence for its diagnostic role. 80. McCormick et al. (1999) compared midazolam and lorazepam for initial seizure treatment, providing evidence for their relative efficacy.
